comment: The decisive mechanism was effective displacement, not the XOR architecture preference. B’s RMSprop lr=0.003 has Δ≈0.77 versus C’s Adagrad Δ≈0.096, and this roughly 8× progress advantage outweighed C’s residual/GELU design. Likewise A’s RMSprop lr=3e-5 (Δ≈0.0077) narrowly beat D’s momentum-SGD lr=1e-4 (Δ≈0.0026), while E was slowest (Δ≈0.0008). K1001’s progress rule helped; I was misled by K1018’s trained-XOR architecture guidance and K1012’s near-chance “tied bottom” heuristic. In XOR lab data, RMSprop .003 beat Adagrad .003 in 18/30 pairs; RMSprop 3e-5 beat SGD 1e-4 in 17/18.
hypothesis: For 8-feature Gaussian XOR at 256×64 (16384 samples), when candidates span optimizer families and remain below clear task saturation, rank primarily by calibrated displacement: RMSprop/Adam Δ≈lr·T, Adagrad Δ≈2lr√T, momentum-SGD Δ≈lr·T·0.01/(1−m). A ≥4× Δ advantage should generally outrank residual/LN/activation differences; within ~3×, architecture can decide. Applied here, estimated Δ ordering is B (.768) > C (.096) > A (.00768) > D (.00256) > E (.000768), matching gold. Backtest on xor lab matched-rate pairs: RMSprop(.003) beat Adagrad(.003) 18/30 (mean CE margin 0.13); RMSprop(3e-5) beat SGD(1e-4) 17/18 (margin 0.054); Adagrad(.003) beat SGD(1e-4) 33/33. These are mixed-architecture comparisons, so the rule is scoped to short-budget XOR selection rather than a universal optimizer law.
